title: Why Dosing Systems Deliver Inconsistent Results
excerpt: Inconsistent dosing can result from product, water, setup, wear, blockage or calibration problems; a structured check is safer than guessing at concentration.
content_html:
A dosing system can make solution preparation more repeatable, but it is not maintenance-free. If output changes from one fill to the next, the cause may be the chemical supply, water conditions, connections, metering components or calibration.

Confirm the product and concentrate supply

Check that the connected concentrate is the approved product for that outlet, is not empty and is within its usable life. A wrong or partially connected container can make the system appear to be a calibration problem when the real issue is product supply.

Check the diluent conditions

Many proportioning systems depend on water flow or pressure within a specified operating range. A significant change in supply conditions can change performance on some designs. Use the manufacturer's troubleshooting process rather than altering plumbing or metering parts without authorisation.

Inspect the approved pickup and metering path

Blocked strainers, kinked tubes, air leaks, worn seals or incorrect metering components can alter concentrate delivery. Only inspect or replace parts identified as user-serviceable in the equipment instructions; other faults should be referred for maintenance.

Calibration can drift or be changed

CDC recommends regular calibration of automatic dispensing systems because a stable-looking dispenser can still prepare the wrong concentration. After maintenance, product changes or unexplained results, verify calibration using the manufacturer's method and any concentration test required by the cleaning programme.

Container and operator choices also matter

Using the wrong fill outlet, changing the intended container size, interrupting a fill cycle or manually adding extra concentrate can defeat a controlled-dosing process. Clear labels and standard operating procedures help keep the preparation step consistent.

Use a controlled troubleshooting sequence

Confirm the product and outlet; inspect visible connections; check water availability; run the prescribed verification or concentration test; then compare the result with the accepted range. If the system remains inconsistent, remove that outlet from use and arrange service rather than compensating by eye.

Practical takeaway

Inconsistent dosing usually means a controllable part of the product, water, setup or maintenance chain has changed. Diagnose the system systematically and verify concentration instead of guessing.

References

  1. CDC — Cleaning Supplies and Equipment.
  2. OSHA — Cleaning Chemicals.
